title: CodeScape
tagline: Developer portal and knowledge graph: every detected technology, capability and relationship carries file, method and confidence.
summary: CodeScape is a developer portal, software catalog and project knowledge graph for code spread across many repositories. A Go API scans local repositories with deterministic parsers and stores entities and relationships in PostgreSQL. A React host loads separately built micro frontends (catalog, 2D graph, 3D universe) at runtime from a plugin registry. The README says nothing detected is shown without provenance, and lists its limits: single node, no authentication, no source-level analysis.

aiRole.summary: AI tooling is documented in the repository. CLAUDE.md is a guidance file for Claude Code (stack, architecture rules, conventions, verification levels), and 18 of the 19 commit messages carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming Claude Opus 5. The original specification (init-prompt.md) and the PE-01 and PE-01.1 milestone briefs are written as prompts to an AI agent, with rules such as not claiming a test passes unless it was run. skills-lock.json records one third-party browser-automation skill. The repository also keeps the milestone reports with commands, counts and a capability matrix that separates code existing, unit tests, end-to-end runs and browser UX checks, so verification steps are documented. That supports 'directed, with documented verification'; this review re-ran none of those checks.

narrative.problem:
The README frames the problem as code that has outgrown one repository: which projects exist and what each does, which technologies are in use and where knowledge is concentrated, which capabilities were built more than once, and what could be reused or connected. The original specification (init-prompt.md) asks for a developer portal, software catalog, project knowledge graph, micro-frontend platform and 3D portfolio in one system, with working code rather than a mock dashboard.

The trust problem is named in ADR 0005: a catalog that quietly guesses is worse than none, so every claim the tool makes has to be checkable.
narrative.approach:
Evidence is part of the domain model, not a display detail. Every detected technology, capability and relationship stores a source, a detection method, a banded confidence and at least one piece of evidence (file, line, snippet, an explanatory sentence). Suggestions are typed apart from observed facts and are never confirmed automatically, and a rejected suggestion is kept so the next scan does not raise it again.

Scanning is deterministic and read-only: parsers read manifests, lockfiles, Dockerfiles, OpenAPI and protobuf documents and directory layout, and never execute repository code. Opportunities come from pure rules. The report lists AI features last, on the ground that the deterministic engine must stay the authority.

Decisions are recorded as seven ADRs: monorepo, a relational graph in PostgreSQL, Module Federation with a runtime registry, local-first scanning, an evidence-first domain, a shared React bridge, and a plugin origin allowlist.
narrative.architecture:
A Go API (chi, pgx, goose migrations, PostgreSQL) holds the domain types, the scanner and normalizer, the analysis rules, the catalog and graph stores and the plugin registry, behind REST under /api/v1 with an OpenAPI document. A React host (apps/web) serves the core pages and loads three separately built remotes at runtime through Module Federation: a catalog, a 2D graph explorer on React Flow and a 3D universe on React Three Fiber. Shared TypeScript packages carry the contracts (types, API client, plugin contract), the design system with its provenance components, and a React bridge for remotes.

The split follows one rule from the micro-frontend doc: anything the product cannot function without belongs in the host, and remotes only add views. The catalog pages, scanning and graph data therefore work with every remote down.
narrative.implementation:
The scanner is an ordered registry of 16 stateless parsers behind a small interface. Findings come from a constructor that requires evidence, snippets are truncated and redacted after credential-shaped keys, and the engine turns a parser panic into a warning. Findings from several parsers are merged with their evidence (capped at five), and the normalizer writes catalog and graph rows only after a scan succeeds. Paths pass one guard that resolves symlinks before testing containment, and git history is read by parsing .git files, never by running git.

The registry is enforced twice. The API checks a remote's origin against an allowlist on register, update and health check. The host checks it again before downloading the code, then checks the host-version range, loads the module with an 8-second timeout, validates the exported shape and collects failures instead of throwing. A failed load is not cached, so Retry refetches. The version-range logic exists once in TypeScript and once in Go.

The graph explorer uses a deterministic layout so a focus command can be tested, and draws unconfirmed edges dashed. The 3D universe keeps camera arithmetic outside React and three.js and renders a list of the same projects beside the canvas.
narrative.outcome:
At the pinned commit the repository holds 19 commits across 2026-07-30 and 2026-07-31, and 18 of them carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming Claude Opus 5. The tree contains 9 Playwright spec files, 18 Go test files under apps/api and 13 TypeScript test files under apps, remotes and packages.

The PE-01.1 report records 188 unit tests, 148 Go tests, 95 Playwright tests and 208 viewport-and-theme passes against a real stack, with one green CI run. Those are the report's figures; this review re-ran none of them. The repository commits no screenshots, because the audit images are gitignored.
narrative.lessons:
What the repo's records say is still open or was learned.

Open: incremental rescanning is the first roadmap item, followed by a per-project world, source-level analysis (call graphs, cross-language AST), scheduled rescans, authentication and team scoping, public GitHub tree scanning and Backstage-compatible export. The API is unauthenticated and single-node, and the threat model calls a parser bug the most plausible vulnerability class. The report's own limits: Chromium only, no assertion on WebGL pixels, one scan at a time, and a small scan fixture.

Learned, as recorded: the PE-01.1 milestone exists because the end-to-end suite described an interface that no longer existed and broke CI on every push while local commands stayed green, and because UI wording did not match behaviour. Universe search removed every unmatched planet while its placeholder promised to focus the camera. A length check counted bytes, so a Thai project name was refused at about 66 characters while an English one was allowed 200.

claims.text: In the domain package, Evidence holds a repository-relative file path, an optional line, a snippet and a human-readable detail. A Relationship stores evidence, source, confidence, detection method, an isConfirmed flag and an optional rejection time.
Confidence is four fixed bands: certain 1.0, high 0.85, medium 0.6 and low 0.35.

Five sources (manual, scanner, metadata, analysis, GitHub) say who asserted a fact, and fifteen detection methods (for example dependency manifest, lockfile, Dockerfile, OpenAPI spec, directory layout, heuristic rule) say how.

Of 19 relationship types, four (COULD_REUSE, COULD_INTEGRATE_WITH, REPLACES, INSPIRED_BY) are marked speculative. The ADR says detected relationships are never auto-confirmed: isConfirmed becomes true only when a person agrees.
Relationship.Status reports DETECTED, CONFIRMED or REJECTED. A rejected edge is kept with a timestamp so the next scan does not raise the same suggestion again.
The scanner is an ordered registry of 16 stateless parsers behind a Parser interface (name, matches, parse). Each parser sees one file; cross-file reasoning happens later, in normalization.

The finding constructor takes an Evidence argument, so every parser finding carries at least one piece of evidence. Snippets are truncated to 200 characters and cut after credential-shaped keys such as password, token and api_key.

The package.json parser records an exact dependency match with certain confidence and a library that only hints at a capability with medium confidence, with a comment that an import does not prove the project implements it.
The engine runs each parser behind a recover, so a panic becomes a warning finding and a partial scan instead of an aborted one.
Findings with the same kind and key from different parsers are merged with their evidence, the highest-confidence detection supplies the value, and evidence is capped at five items.

Every repository path goes through safepath.Resolve: absolute, no NUL bytes, an existing directory, symlinks resolved before the containment test, and containment by filepath.Rel so a sibling with a shared prefix is rejected. The engine re-validates the path although its callers already did.

The walker skips dependency, build and hidden folders (except .github and .codescape), stops at depth, file-count and file-size limits, drops symlinked files that resolve outside the allowed roots, and records a partial run with a warning instead of failing.
readFile re-checks the size and reads at most limit plus one byte, so a file that grows after discovery cannot slip past the limit and a short read cannot silently yield truncated input.

Git history is read by parsing .git files (HEAD, refs, packed-refs, loose commit objects); the git binary is never invoked because a repository controls its own .git/config. Packed objects are not read, so commit time falls back to the ref file's modification time and is marked approximate.

The normalizer writes catalog and graph rows only after a scan produced findings. It first clears what the previous scan asserted, keeping manual assertions, and it never infers a capability's maturity from a parser.
Opportunity rules are pure functions over a snapshot of the catalog, and results are sorted by impact then key so repeated runs match. The package comment says no AI or heuristic scoring is involved.

A remote exports a plugin object with id, name, version and compatibleHostVersions, plus optional routes, widgets, project tabs and commands; the host passes it a context with an API client, theme and reduced-motion flag.

The host never imports a remote statically. loadPlugins checks the origin allowlist before anything is fetched, then the declared host-version range, loads the module with an 8-second timeout, validates the exported shape, re-checks the remote's own range, and collects every failure instead of throwing.
A failed remote load is not cached, so Retry refetches. Successful loads are cached by entry URL and module so a StrictMode double render does not evaluate a remote twice.

The Go registry applies the same origin guard on register, update and health check, requires a guard at construction (nil becomes deny-all), refuses to delete built-in remotes, and treats an empty allowlist as deny-all.

Registry changes are authorised separately from origin checks: CODESCAPE_PLUGIN_MANAGEMENT defaults to disabled, which makes the registry read-only over HTTP. The ADR lists Content-Security-Policy headers on the host as a residual risk that is not yet implemented.
Host-version compatibility exists twice: isHostVersionCompatible in TypeScript, whose comment says it is shared with the API, and Service.compatible in Go, which has its own 16-case table test.
A host unit test reads package.json, plugin.tsx and main.go to check that each remote's package version equals its plugin version and that its declared host range covers the API's host version.

Remotes alias react, react-dom and the JSX runtime to bridge modules in packages/mfe-runtime instead of using Module Federation's shared option, because shared cannot see require('react') inside CommonJS dependencies.
Anything the product cannot function without lives in the host. Playwright tests abort one remote, all remotes or the registry request and assert that core pages still load.

The graph layout is deterministic (projects on a circle, other nodes orbiting their owner) so that a focus command can be tested; unconfirmed or speculative edges are drawn dashed and rejected ones faded.

Graph search ranks exact, prefix, then substring matches and breaks ties by degree. focusCommand returns null for an unknown node so the viewport is left alone, and moves with zero duration under reduced motion.

In the 3D universe each domain is a galaxy placed on a ring and each project a planet sized by connectivity, clamped to 2.6. Camera goals are plain arithmetic outside React and three.js. Without WebGL it falls back to a 2D list, and the accessible project list renders either way.

Go (chi, cors, pgx, goose, yaml.v3) owns scanning, graph storage, analysis and the plugin registry behind REST under /api/v1. A Go test fails the build if a registered route is missing from the OpenAPI document.
CI defines four jobs: lint, typecheck, test and build for the frontend; go build, vet and test with -race; Docker image builds; and Playwright end-to-end against a real API and PostgreSQL.

The PE-01.1 report records 188 unit tests, 148 Go tests and a Playwright run of 95 tests across nine spec files, with a capability matrix. These are the report's figures; this review re-ran none of them.
The report gives its premise as a stale end-to-end suite that broke CI on every push for at least two commits while local commands stayed green, with three UI claims that were untrue.
One recorded defect: a length check counted bytes, so a Thai project name was refused at about 66 characters while an English one was allowed 200. The report says the fix counts characters instead.
The report states its own limits: Chromium only, no test asserts what a pixel in the WebGL output looks like, one scan at a time on one API, and the scan fixture is small.

The README lists these limits: one in-process worker pool with no distributed lock, an unauthenticated API for trusted networks, a scanner that reads manifests and structure but does not build call graphs, GitHub import that catalogs metadata only, and no per-project world yet.
The threat model lists no authentication or authorization as a limit and says a parsing bug is the most plausible vulnerability class, because parsers process untrusted input.
The README roadmap puts incremental rescanning first (hash file contents, skip unchanged files). The PE-01.1 report lists AI features as deliberately last.
The repository has 19 commits, all by one author name, 9 on 2026-07-30 and 10 on 2026-07-31.
18 commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming Claude Opus 5.
The tree has 9 Playwright spec files, 18 Go test files under apps/api and 13 TypeScript test files under apps, remotes and packages. These are file counts, not test results.

CLAUDE.md addresses Claude Code. The specification (init-prompt.md) and the PE-01 and PE-01.1 briefs are written as prompts to an AI agent; the PE-01 brief says not to claim a test passes unless it was run, and CLAUDE.md says never to claim something works unless it was executed.
skills-lock.json records one installed skill, ego-browser, from the public repository citrolabs/ego-lite, with a content hash.

CLAUDE.md states two rules the AI tooling works under: detected data must never render as confirmed fact, and deterministic parsing is primary with AI not the repository parser. It points to the PE-01.1 capability matrix as the record of which verification level each feature reached.

The federation plugin emits remoteEntry.js only during a build, so pnpm dev serves built previews of the remotes and a change inside a remote needs a rebuild. A Playwright test checks that each remote entry is served as JavaScript rather than the SPA fallback.

excerpts.title: Evidence and confidence are domain types
excerpts.why: Evidence carries a repository-relative path, a line, a short snippet and a sentence a developer can check. Confidence is four fixed bands, so a directory-name heuristic cannot be reported at the same level as an exact dependency match.

excerpts.title: Detected, confirmed and rejected edges
excerpts.why: A relationship stores its evidence, source, confidence and method next to isConfirmed. RejectedAt separates 'not yet reviewed' from 'reviewed and rejected', and Status() derives the label, so a dismissed suggestion is retained rather than deleted.

excerpts.title: Parser interface and ordered registry
excerpts.why: Each parser sees one file and returns findings; the registry is a plain ordered list of 16 implementations. Cross-file reasoning is deliberately left to normalization.

excerpts.title: Merging findings and capping evidence
excerpts.why: The same technology found by several parsers becomes one finding that keeps all the evidence. The highest-confidence detection supplies the value, and evidence is cut to five items.

excerpts.title: Resolve symlinks before testing containment
excerpts.why: The comment on filepath.Clean says cleaning alone is not protection; EvalSymlinks runs before the check against the allowed roots, so a link inside a root that points outside is rejected.

excerpts.title: Per-remote checks before a remote runs
excerpts.why: A disabled remote is skipped, then the origin is checked before anything is fetched, then the declared host-version range. Each failure is pushed to a result list with a reason instead of thrown.

excerpts.title: Unconfirmed edges look unconfirmed
excerpts.why: Confirmed edges are green and solid; unconfirmed or speculative edges are dashed; rejected ones are faded. The provenance model reaches the pixels.

excerpts.title: Camera goal as plain arithmetic
excerpts.why: The goal is computed outside React and three.js so it can be unit-tested; distance scales with planet radius and is floored at the OrbitControls minimum.

limitations: Single node: scans run in an in-process worker pool and there is no distributed lock (README).
No authentication: the API is unauthenticated and assumes a trusted network; do not expose it to the internet as-is (README, threat model).

The scanner reads manifests, lockfiles, interfaces, metadata and structure, not source; it builds no call graphs and does no AST analysis, and capability detection from dependencies is shallow (README).
Packed git objects are not read; commit times fall back to the ref file's modification time and are marked approximate (README).
GitHub or Git import catalogs metadata only; remote code is never fetched or parsed, so analysis needs a registered local path (README).
There is no per-project world yet: repository folder districts, source-level call graphs and a navigable per-project 3D world are not implemented (README).
Plugin registry: Content-Security-Policy headers on the host are not implemented; registry changes are read-only over HTTP unless a management token is configured (ADR 0007).

Threat-model limits: local paths are visible to anyone who can reach the API, there is no multi-tenancy, rate limiting is per-process and in memory, and parsers process untrusted input (docs/security/threat-model.md).

Verification limits recorded in the PE-01.1 report: Chromium only, no assertion on WebGL pixels, scan concurrency untested at scale, a small scan fixture. The test figures shown here are the report's and were not re-run.
pnpm dev serves the remotes from built previews, so a change inside a remote needs a rebuild (README).
The repository commits no screenshots (the UX-audit images are gitignored), so none are shown here.
